summary: The meaning, mode, recipients, and significance of baptism as a sign and seal of the New Covenant
readingInstruction: Read Matthew 28:18-20, Romans 6:1-4, Acts 2:38-41, and Colossians 2:11-12. Today is a doctrinal pause on baptism. Notice what each passage says baptism pictures and what it commits us to.
settingTheScene: Jesus commanded baptism as part of making disciples. The early church practiced it from the first day: in Acts 2, three thousand were baptized after Peter’s sermon. In his letters, Paul explains what baptism means. Christians have disagreed about some aspects of baptism, particularly about who should be baptized and the mode. This lesson focuses on what the Scriptures say about its meaning, and notes where traditions differ.
observation: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).
“Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?” (Romans 6:3).
“We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death” (Romans 6:4).
“So that… we too might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4).
“Repent and be baptized every one of you in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins” (Acts 2:38).
“And you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38).
“So those who received his word were baptized, and there were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41).
“Having been buried with him in baptism, in which you were also raised with him through faith in the powerful working of God” (Colossians 2:12).
doctrinalFocus: Baptism is the sign, commanded by Christ, of entrance into the new covenant community. It pictures union with Christ in his death and resurrection, the washing away of sin, and the gift of the Spirit, and it publicly marks a person as belonging to the triune God and his people. Baptism does not save by itself; salvation comes by grace through faith. But baptism is not optional, for it is Christ’s command and the normal response of faith. Christians have differed on whether the proper subjects are believers only, or also the infant children of believers, and on the mode of baptism. Reformed churches have held both views. All agree that baptism is a gift to be received with faith and that it points to Christ.
interpretation:
Baptism begins with a command. After the resurrection, Jesus told the disciples to make disciples by baptizing and teaching. It is not an extra for the especially devoted but a normal part of becoming a disciple. It is done in the name of the triune God, which means the person is brought under the ownership and protection of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

Romans 6 gives the central meaning. Paul is answering the question, “Should we continue in sin that grace may abound?” He says no, because in baptism we were united with Christ in his death and burial, and raised to walk in newness of life. Baptism is a picture of the gospel: death to the old life and resurrection to the new. Colossians 2:11-12 says the same: buried with him in baptism and raised with him through faith. The faith is key. Baptism is a sign of what God does for those who believe.

On the day of Pentecost, Peter says to repent and be baptized for the forgiveness of sins, and promises the gift of the Spirit. Baptism goes with repentance and faith. Notice that the promise is “for you and for your children,” which is where the different traditions find support for their practice. Those who baptize only professing believers see baptism as the outward sign of an inward faith that has already begun. Those who baptize infants of believers see it as a covenant sign like circumcision, promising what God will do. Both agree that the sign is empty without faith and that the reality is Christ.

For a new believer, baptism is a joyful step. If you have not been baptized, talk with your pastor. If you have, remember it: you were marked as Christ’s.
connection: Genesis 17:9-14 describes circumcision as the sign of the old covenant. Galatians 3:26-29 says all who are baptized into Christ have put on Christ. 1 Peter 3:21 says baptism now saves you as an appeal to God for a good conscience through the resurrection of Jesus. Acts 8:36-39 and 16:31-34 record baptisms. Titus 3:5. Ephesians 4:4-6 speaks of one Lord, one faith, one baptism. Mark 16:16.
application:
If you have not been baptized, speak to a pastor or leader about it this week.

If you have been baptized, remember the day, and thank God for the promise it signified.

When you struggle with sin, remember Romans 6: you are united with Christ, dead to sin and alive to God.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for baptism and what it shows about your washing and new life.
Tell him where you need to remember your baptism.
Pray for those who have not been baptized.
